title: When the Bell Burns
premise: Rosalind Eriksen, a property surveyor who has spent her life making herself unremarkable, is sent to appraise Hollowmere House, a colonial estate whose previous owners all vanished on closing day. The house's mirrors lag one second behind reality, and in that stolen second Rosalind glimpses a version of herself that stayed—braver, louder, and slowly replacing her. She learns the town's founders built the house as a vessel for an exchange ritual: it trades one resident's existence for the community's prosperity, and the sale papers are the signature. To survive, Rosalind must complete the founders' interrupted counter-ritual before signing, sacrificing her invisibility—and the mirror-self—to become someone the house cannot swallow. In the end she signs as herself, and the house, denied its echo, goes dark.
about_author: Dominic Marchetti spent fifteen years as a building inspector in upstate New York, where he collected the strange histories of houses no one wanted to buy. He writes horror about ordinary professionals who discover their paperwork has teeth.

chapters.title: The Listing
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. A property surveyor famous for being forgettable takes the Hollowmere House appraisal no one else will touch. The emotional beat is quiet unease: she measures every room twice because the numbers refuse to match, and the house feels like it is measuring her back.

chapters.title: Square Footage of Nothing
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Her survey shows a room that exists on no blueprint—a narrow space between the walls, warm to the touch. The beat is professional denial; she files the anomaly and tells herself old houses settle. That night, a door she counted shut stands open.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. In the hallway mirror, her reflection moves a heartbeat after she does. She tests it with a dropped pen, then with a scream. The beat is creeping dread: the lag isn't a glitch—it's attention. Something in the glass is learning her timing.

chapters.title: The Previous Owners
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind, with archival documents. At the county records office she finds four prior sales of Hollowmere, each closed and each buyer untraceable afterward—no death record, no forwarding address, just a signature. The beat is cold realization: the house doesn't kill its residents. It erases them.

chapters.title: Doors Counted
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Her coping rituals—lights on, doors tallied—begin failing; the house has one more door each morning than the night before. The beat is loss of control. Her systems for staying invisible were never habits. They were wards, inherited from a mother who knew what houses could do.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Stayed
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. In the lagging reflection she sees not her own delay but another woman entirely—her face, but confident, smiling, wearing clothes Rosalind would never dare. The beat is vertigo: the mirror isn't showing the past. It's showing the self she refused to become, waiting its turn.

chapters.title: Hollowmere's Founders
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind, interleaved with 1840s letters from founder Abigail Voss. The letters reveal the town's founding bargain: a house built as a vessel, one resident exchanged each generation for the valley's fortune, the ritual left deliberately unfinished so the house must keep asking. The beat is horrified comprehension.

chapters.title: Closing Date
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Her firm calls: an anonymous buyer wants to close in nine days, and her appraisal is the last requirement. The beat is trap-springing—she was never surveying the house. She was preparing it for sale, and her signature starts the clock.

chapters.title: What the Valley Got
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind among the townspeople. Hollowmere's neighbors are unnervingly prosperous, unnervingly insistent that she stay for dinner, stay the night, stay forever. The beat is loyalty versus truth: these kind people are beneficiaries of the exchange, and some of them know exactly what they're feeding.

chapters.title: The Second Room
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. She finally enters the between-walls room and finds the founders' ritual circle, half-carved and abandoned, along with four sets of clothing folded neatly—each previous owner got this far. The beat is despair edged with defiance: they stopped because finishing meant giving something up.

chapters.title: Mirror Work
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Experimenting at night, she learns the lag widens when she lies about herself and narrows when she speaks truths aloud. The house feeds on concealment; her lifelong invisibility has been seasoning her. The beat is painful self-recognition disguised as research.

chapters.title: The Buyer
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. The anonymous buyer arrives early: a smooth man whose reflection arrives a full second before he does. He is the house's agent, or its mouth, and he compliments her thoroughness. The beat is open menace—the transaction wants a willing seller, and he intends to make her willing.

chapters.title: Abigail's Last Letter
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Hidden in the second room, Abigail Voss's final letter confesses she couldn't finish the counter-ritual because it requires the resident to be fully seen—name, history, every shame spoken into the circle. Abigail chose the town over herself. The beat is the theme made flesh: survival costs identity either way.

chapters.title: Interference
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. The town closes ranks: roads washed out, her phone dead, her firm suddenly unreachable. The buyer hosts a welcome dinner where everyone toasts her 'new beginning.' The beat is isolation tightening—loyalty here means complicity, and leaving is no longer offered.

chapters.title: The Other Rosalind Speaks
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. The mirror-self steps fully out of sync, speaking in the glass: she offers a trade—let me take the signature, take the life, and you can go back to being no one, safe forever. The beat is temptation. It is everything Rosalind has ever wanted: to disappear without dying.

chapters.title: Small Treasons
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Exhausted, she nearly accepts, nearly signs a preliminary consent form the buyer slides across the dinner table. One of the townspeople—an old woman with no reflection at all—slips her a warning note: 'It keeps the ones who half-choose.' The beat is a hand reaching through the dark.

chapters.title: The Unreflected
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. The old woman, Mirabel, reveals she was the fifth owner who escaped mid-ritual by refusing to choose—but the house kept her reflection as collateral. She becomes Rosalind's reluctant ally. The beat is fragile loyalty: two damaged women deciding whether truth between them is worth the risk.

chapters.title: Nine Doors
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. With two days to closing, the house turns hostile outright: walls rearrange, the second room seals itself, and the mirror-self begins appearing outside the glass, walking the halls in Rosalind's gait. The beat is siege. The house is done courting; it is herding.

chapters.title: Everything Spoken
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Rosalind breaks into the reopened circle and begins the counter-ritual: naming herself completely—her mother's wards, her cowardices, the sister she let vanish from her life rather than be seen failing. The beat is raw catharsis. Each truth spoken shrinks the mirror-lag; each one costs her the armor of anonymity.

chapters.title: The Signing
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Closing day. The buyer presents the papers; the mirror-self stands beside him, offering the easy trade one last time. Rosalind refuses, completes the circle's final line with her full name aloud, and signs the sale as herself—not the house's echo, not a ghost, a person. The beat is climax: visibility as weapon.

chapters.title: What the House Kept
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. The exchange reverses: the mirror-self is pulled back into the glass and held there, the buyer unravels into dust and old signatures, and the house exhales a century of borrowed luck. Mirabel's reflection returns to her face. The beat is aftermath-shock—victory that feels like bereavement, because part of her died in that glass.

chapters.title: Appraised at Last
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Weeks later, Rosalind files her report declaring Hollowmere unsellable and watches the town's prosperity dim without rancor—they will have to earn it now. She calls her sister. The beat is resolution: she keeps the lights on out of habit now, not fear, and when she passes a mirror, she arrives exactly on time.
